headline: Treasury yields surged, lifting the 10-year to 5.10%, as stocks slipped on Jensen Huang's abrupt exit from Nvidia and oil jumped on fresh Gulf attacks.
dateline: Friday, November 13, 2026 · closes as of Thu Nov 12

rundown.h: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia.
rundown.p: Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO Thursday, Reuters reported, with CFO Colette Kress named interim chief. The stock fell as much as 14% intraday before closing down 4.34% at $166.19, and Bernstein halved its price target to $200. The company that anchors the AI trade now reports third-quarter results Nov. 17 without its founder at the helm.

rundown.h: The 30-year auction tailed, the week's third.
rundown.p: The Treasury's $25 billion 30-year sale cleared at 5.441%, above the 5.437% when-issued yield, with indirect bidders taking 68.1%, their smallest share since August, and bid-to-cover slipping to 2.36. The 3- and 10-year sales also tailed this week. Soft demand at the long end keeps pressure on the yields that price commercial mortgages.

rundown.h: Markets now treat a December hike as done.
rundown.p: CME FedWatch showed full odds of a December rate increase Thursday, with about a 13% chance of a half-point move, and Goldman Sachs now expects another quarter-point hike in March, CNBC reported. Cleveland's Hammack said she prefers smaller, more frequent hikes, and Chicago's Goolsbee declined to signal the size of the next move.

Initial claims rose to 200,000 in the week ended Nov. 7, above the 195,000 forecast and up from a revised 191,000, per Trading Economics; the four-week average was 195,250. Layoffs remain historically low, which keeps the labor market from giving the Fed a reason to pause.

rundown.h: U.S. fuel stocks built across the board.
rundown.p: EIA data for the week to Nov. 6 showed commercial crude inventories up 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million, gasoline up 1.8 million and distillates, which include diesel, up 4.1 million to 103.3 million. Rising distillate stocks are the first thing that would ease diesel prices for truckers heading into winter.

rundown.h: Individual investors are the gloomiest in months.
rundown.p: The AAII sentiment survey put bulls at 30.8% and bears at 51.4%, a bearish spread of 20.6 points, even with major indexes near record territory. Contrarians often read lopsided pessimism like this as a sign that much of the bad news is already priced.

dive.title: The AI boom just showed up on your electric bill
dive.dek: Big Tech is spending at a record pace on data centers, and the grid, ratepayers and anyone leasing power-hungry space are starting to pay for it.
body: Start with the latest CPI. In the October report released Nov. 10, the BLS electricity index rose 0.9% in one month, more than double the 0.4% rise in overall prices. The same day, the EIA's November outlook had the average residential rate climbing from 17.2¢/kWh in 2025 to 18.2¢ this year and 18.7¢ in 2027, driven mainly by commercial demand, the category that includes data centers.

The spending behind that demand is enormous. In the September quarter Amazon spent $77.3 billion on property and equipment, Alphabet $51.4 billion and Microsoft $45.2 billion; Meta's 2026 forecast is $135 billion to $145 billion. Cash flow alone no longer covers it. Alphabet sold $28.7 billion of senior notes in the quarter, and Microsoft carries $364.6 billion of leases that haven't started yet, mostly for data centers. AI capex is now a credit story as much as a tech story.

The grid is where the bill lands. PJM, the largest U.S. grid operator, serving 67 million people, saw its latest capacity auction clear at the $325/MW-day cap, $16.4 billion in all, and still come up 6,831 MW short of its reliability target (July 14). PJM's market monitor attributes about 46% of capacity costs over the last four auctions, roughly $29.4 billion, to data centers, and Dallas Fed researchers estimate existing data centers have already lifted wholesale power prices 2% to 6% nationally. Utilities forecast about 90 GW of new data-center load by 2030; market analysts put it nearer 65 GW. If the analysts are right, some of the grid now being planned may never be needed.

Regulators are starting to make big users pay their own way: Oregon approved rates that lift data-center bills about 29% while trimming residential rates 1.3%, and Ohio and Virginia have special tariffs for loads of 25 MW and up. For industrial real estate, power is becoming the binding site constraint. Sites with secured power and the transmission to deliver it are worth more, and owners of manufacturing and logistics buildings in PJM territory face higher utility pass-throughs and harder lease talks over who pays them. What would change the picture: slower AI spending, or load forecasts falling toward the analysts' lower numbers.

items.title: October existing home sales fell 5.5% to 3.75 million, the fewest since August 2010
body: Sales of previously owned homes fell 5.5% in October to a 3.75 million annual pace, below the 3.85 million consensus and the revised 3.97 million September pace, NAR said Nov. 12. Sales were down 8.8% from a year earlier and have slid from 4.27 million last December. The West led the drop, down 9.7% on the month and 14.5% on the year; the Northeast was flat.

Prices held up even as volume fell: the median was $416,700, up 0.4% from a year earlier. Inventory rose 4.6% from a year ago to 1.59 million, or 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.7 in September. First-time buyers fell to 29% of sales from 31%, cash deals rose to 29%, and homes sat 35 days, up from 33. NAR cited Freddie Mac's 30-year rate averaging 7.33% in October, against 6.25% a year earlier.
Treasury yields rose sharply the same day, with the 10-year up about 13 basis points, though CNBC tied the move to oil and Fed hike bets rather than housing.

experts.who: Lawrence Yun, chief economist, National Association of Realtors
experts.view: Blames mortgage rates near their highest since 2000 for the slump and says lower rates could release a lot of pent-up demand.
Says the Fed's inflation fight is pushing housing from a correction toward a severe downturn, with buyers largely absent.

items.lean: Yun sees rates as the main obstacle and pent-up demand waiting; Rupkey expects the Fed's hikes to deepen the slump.

lead.title: The Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's Hormuz bypass as Iran claims a mine struck an LNG carrier
lead.body:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said Nov. 12 they attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, an oil facility in the Red Sea port of Yanbu and an Aramco building in Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones, one over the Riyadh region and one over the Eastern Province. The pipeline to Yanbu is the kingdom's main export route that avoids the Strait of Hormuz (Reuters, Nov 12).

Early Nov. 13, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said an LNG carrier hit a mine east of the strait and exploded, a day after the army claimed two more tankers caught fire; none of the claims was independently verified, and the U.S. military says it has cleared the strait's routes of mines. On Nov. 12 Iran's Assembly of Experts urged leaders to weigh leaving the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, and President Trump posted that the U.S. does not need a deal with Iran (CBS News).
lead.reach: Through oil: Brent settled up $3.06, or 3.3%, at $95.82 on Nov. 12, yet was still down about 2.5% on the week (Reuters, Nov 12); CBS puts oil more than 40% above prewar levels. Hits to the bypass routes raise the floor under fuel, freight and inflation expectations, and with them Treasury yields.

views.who: Daan Struyven and Yulia Zhestkova Grigsby, Goldman Sachs
views.view: See substantial downside risks to supply justifying a large near-term risk premium, and raised their December Brent forecast to $105 from $90.

views.who: Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson, ING
views.view: Say the market has been unwinding part of the war risk premium built up in recent weeks, while staying sensitive to Middle East headlines.

reading.title: Sam Zell, the Grave Dancer
reading.dek: A refugees' son from Chicago bought what other investors had given up on, helped bring REITs back, and showed how debt can both build a fortune and wreck a deal.
body: Sam Zell's story begins with an escape. His Polish-Jewish parents fled Europe and reached the United States about four months before he was born in Chicago on September 28, 1941, having crossed Russia and Japan on transit visas issued by Japanese diplomat Chiune Sugihara. Born Shmuel Zielonka, he became one of the most inventive and outspoken property investors of the postwar era, a man who cheerfully called himself the Grave Dancer.

His career started on campus. As a University of Michigan student he managed a 15-unit apartment building in exchange for room and board, and the side job grew quickly enough to net him $150,000 by graduation. By the time he finished law school in 1966, he and partner Robert Lurie were overseeing more than 4,000 apartments. He practiced law for roughly a week before concluding real estate was the better business. In 1969 he founded the predecessor of what became Equity Residential, and in 1976 the forerunner of Equity Office.

The nickname came from an essay he wrote for Real Estate Review explaining his method: buy the distressed properties others have abandoned, but never get so close to the wreckage that you fall in yourself. He preferred discipline to glamour, avoiding trophy buildings, auctions and outdated office space. He also helped revive the real estate investment trust as a way to raise public money instead of guaranteeing deals with his own assets. Equity Residential went public in August 1993, and in 2007 Zell sold Equity Office to Blackstone in what was then the largest leveraged buyout ever.

That same year produced his best-known stumble. Zell led a leveraged buyout of the Tribune Company valued at roughly $8 billion, contributing $315 million of his own capital. Unable to carry its debt load, Tribune filed for bankruptcy in December 2008, the largest in U.S. media history, and Zell lost his investment. The contrast with his property wins is the lesson: borrowing that suits buildings with steady rents can sink a business whose cash flow is shrinking.

Zell died on May 18, 2023, at 81, with Forbes estimating his fortune at about $5.2 billion. His most-repeated principle was that cash and access to capital are what let an investor act when everyone else is forced to sell, which is exactly when the best bargains appear. He set out his views in a 2017 book, Am I Being Too Subtle?, a fitting title for a man rarely accused of subtlety.

quote.src: Sam Zell, a favorite maxim (via Fortune, 2023)

takeaways: With the 10-year above 5%, leverage on shrinking cash flows is the Tribune trap.
Keep dry powder: forced sellers create the bargains a grave dancer waits for.
A December hike rewards balance sheets that can carry debt through a downturn.
